title: The Ceiling on Fractional: When a Growing Business Needs a Full-Time CFO
linkedin:
An owner asked us recently, almost apologetically: "Does needing more from you mean we've outgrown you?"

It usually means the opposite of what they fear.

A fractional CFO relationship that's working well eventually points to its own ceiling. That's not a failure of the model, it's the model doing exactly what it was built to do.

The clearest signal isn't revenue. It's decision cadence.

We see it when a business that once made two or three material financial calls a month is suddenly making two or three a week. Pricing decisions, hiring approvals, supplier negotiations, all needing input in real time rather than at the next scheduled session. A part-time presence, however senior, starts to lag the business rather than lead alongside it.

The businesses that handle this transition well don't treat it as an exit. They treat it as a handover. The dashboards, the monthly rhythm, the forecasting discipline, all of it is designed to outlive the engagement, not get rebuilt from scratch by whoever comes next.

Most owners never reach this point, and that's a perfectly good outcome too. But for the ones scaling past it, naming the ceiling early makes the transition far smoother than waiting until a gap in leadership is already costing something.

A question we hear a lot from growing businesses across Brisbane and the East Coast: how do you know when it's time to move from part-time financial support to a full-time hire?

The answer usually isn't about revenue. It's about how often financial decisions are actually being made. When a business shifts from a couple of material calls a month to several a week, pricing changes, hiring approvals, supplier terms, a part-time cadence starts to lag behind the pace the business is moving at.

The businesses that make this shift well treat it as a proper handover rather than a sudden exit, so the reporting rhythm and forecasting discipline already in place don't get lost along the way. It's a good problem to have, and one worth planning for rather than reacting to.
